name: Max Weber
role: German sociologist, political economist and publicist (1864-1920)
summary: German liberal-nationalist political economist and sociologist who put the power interests of the nation state above economic class interests and argued for a strong parliament and a directly elected, plebiscitary president as the way to select political leaders against rule by officials. He saw modern life as bureaucratising and disenchanted, held that conflicting ultimate values cannot be settled by science or reason, and doubted that socialism could do more than extend bureaucracy.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He rejected pacifism for a Machtstaat like Germany and said no amount of pacifist talk alters its duty; only small states such as Switzerland could rely on a militia.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He argued that eliminating money and capital accounting brings an unavoidable loss of calculatory rationality.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: He condemned Bismarck's anti-Socialist law, which denied socialists the rights of assembly and publication, as a political blunder that fed radicalism.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: He called the budget the most important task of parliament and the foundation of the power of a people's assembly, and rejected deciding it by referendum.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: He treated organised parties as unavoidable in mass democracy and wanted leaders to rise through them and parliament, not around them.

central-planning.rationale: In Economy and Society he held that a planned economy lacks an instrument of rational calculation and loses formal rationality by eliminating money accounting.

class-struggle-history.rationale: He took Marx's ideas as suggestive ideal types, said politics and power struggles between nations are autonomous, and not a reflection of class interest.

collective-bargaining.rationale: He described the unions' fight over working conditions as the workers' own representation of their interests, which the state should not obstruct.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He called Bismarck's pensions for the sick, injured and old admirable, though in his view they were too little without guarantees for workers' independence.

decide-locally.rationale: He argued the Reich needed a unifying head against particularism and Prussian hegemony and rejected dissolving Germany into small Swiss-style cantons.

democracy-becomes-oligarchy.rationale: He held that policy is always made by a small number of people and that mass democracy always pays with concessions to the leader principle.

democracy-best.rationale: He accepted democracy as a fact and defended equal suffrage and a strong parliament, but did not treat it as an absolute value and feared leaderless, bureaucratic mass democracy.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: He described politics and parliament as conflict, recruitment of allies and a voluntary following, and valued party struggle as the way leaders are selected.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: In his 1918 lecture 'Socialism' he judged the Bolshevik dictatorship a military dictatorship of corporals and the experiment unpromising, saying the dictatorship of the official, not the worker, was advancing.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: In 'The President of the Reich' (1919) he argued that the head of state must be elected directly by the whole people, not by parliament.

direct-votes.rationale: He argued that referenda on laws and budgets would be a mechanical brake on progress in a mass state because they rule out compromise, allowing them only for simple yes-or-no questions or as a corrective.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He held the German 'race' should be protected in the east, which implies a German character for that region, but did not state a general rule.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: He wanted the popularly elected president to hold a delaying veto and the power to dissolve parliament and consult the people.

hereditarian-race.rationale: His 1895 lecture treated Germans' and Poles' difference in adaptability as a fixed given; his later work calls the heredity of racial traits unsettled and of little social effect.

independent-unions.rationale: He blamed Bismarck for using the police and the anti-Socialist law to smash the unions, which he said drove members into party-political radicalism.

majority-settlement.rationale: In 1895 he demanded systematic state colonisation of the eastern provinces by German peasants to Germanise districts with a Polish population.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He described the market economy as the form with exact money calculation and a strong incentive to labour, which a planned economy lacks, while noting substantive-rationality problems.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: He held that politics is never a mere superstructure of the material base and that freedom survives only through a nation's will against the tide of material constellations.

means-match-ends.rationale: He held that no ethic can avoid the fact that good ends often require morally suspect or dangerous means.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He accepted monarchs as formal heads under a sovereign parliament and said they should stay out of party struggle, but he also said monarchy guarantees nothing.

multipolar-world.rationale: He argued that Germany must resist the division of world power between Russian officialdom and English-speaking society.

nation-first.rationale: He declared that the ultimate interests economic policy must serve are those of national power, and his wartime writings put the nation's historical tasks above the form of the state.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: He argued that a directly elected president could stand above party and regional divisions and represent the unity of the Reich.

organic-representation.rationale: He held that representation by occupational estates has no proper place in parliamentary elections and criticised occupational associations dictating party lists.

parliament-supreme.rationale: He held that full parliamentary power is indispensable wherever hereditary monarchs head the officials, since a monarch cannot control administration, and demanded a sovereign parliament.

participatory-democracy.rationale: He held direct democracy technically unworkable in large states and doubted obligatory referenda and endless popular elections as political education; small cantons were a different case.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: He held that Germany had a duty to defend its culture and that a German economic policy must serve German values, while saying small states may cultivate culture as well.

property-franchise.rationale: In 'Suffrage and Democracy in Germany' he called the Prussian three-class franchise untenable and said any franchise other than equal suffrage would wrong the returning soldiers.

proportional-representation.rationale: He criticised proportional representation in its present form as a feature of leaderless democracy that fills parliament with pressure-group officials.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In his 1895 inaugural lecture he demanded the closing of the eastern frontier to Polish migratory labour; the demand is from his early career and not revisited later.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: He held that workers' economic struggles must be given free rein as a moral force and criticised the state's repression of the unions.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He urged the ethic of responsibility, judging action by its foreseeable consequences, though he held it complements an ethic of conviction.

separate-church-state.rationale: He wrote that state-run dogmatic and apologetic theology serves only the state's wish for cultural regulation and that an inevitable separation of church and state would be in the interest of religious life too.

single-common-good.rationale: He held that conflicting ultimate values are irreconcilable ('polytheism') and that no ethic or science can decide among them.

state-class-instrument.rationale: He defined the state by its monopoly of legitimate force, not by serving a class, and treated the political sphere as autonomous.

state-harmful.rationale: He treated the state as the worldly organisation of the nation's power and its power as the ultimate criterion of economic policy.

strong-leader.rationale: He wanted a popularly elected Reich president able to act in crises (delaying veto, dissolving parliament, calling a referendum) as a counterweight to a leaderless parliament, while bound by the law.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In 1895 he spoke of the 'elbow-room' won for descendants and German world power, but during the First World War he opposed annexations in Europe.

unions-good.rationale: In 'Parliament and Government' he called the trade unions the only institutions that could objectively represent workers' interests and said the sense of honour and comradeship in workers' economic struggles must be given free rein.

unions-run-economy.rationale: He argued that trade unionists lack the knowledge to run factories and would depend on non-workers, so syndicalist control of production was unlikely to work.

universal-morality.rationale: He denied that any value system can be shown by reason to be right: the various value systems are in unresolvable conflict.

workers-councils.rationale: He argued parliament must rest on equal suffrage representing citizens' needs, not their place in production, and that an occupational-estate structure has no place where the voting slip rules.

notes: Texts read from the maintainer-supplied books by searching each theme: nation and economic policy, immigration and settlement, suffrage, parliament and budget, referendum, president, federalism, socialism and syndicalism, unions and welfare, church and state, planned economy, value pluralism, war and pacifism, race and ethnicity, monarchy. The Cambridge volume's page numbers are not cited because the local text is an OCR conversion. Weber's nationalism moderated after 1895 (editors); the 1895 immigration and settlement positions are therefore medium. Most statements concern topics Weber never addressed (family, sexuality, drugs, environment, technology, religion policy) and are null.
